name: Skills
text:
In this workshop, you will develop a better understanding of what your skills are. You will become more acquainted with what you are good at compared to other people. In general, there are three types of skills. The first is something that you learned to do well - something that you are good or proficient at. The second is something that gives you a competitive edge. This could be something that you trained at and, as a result of your practice, you are better than most people at. Although slightly rare, the third is something that you do better than anyone that you have ever met. These skills are distinct and, if harnessed and amplified out in the right way, can lead to a distinct competitive advantage. 

Activity

In your journal, write out the answers to the following questions. As suggested, neuroscientists suggest writing out the activities as opposed to typing them out. Writing is much better in helping us to build more neural pathways in our mind compared to typing. 

What are your main skills? What are your biggest strengths? What do you do better than anyone else? What is your individual competitive advantage?

In addition to discovering these facets of yourself through the meditation, ask three people that you are close with to share with you what they consider to be your main strengths. Compare these lists with the list that you have compiled through the activity and the subsequent meditation.

name: Limitations
text:
In this workshop, you develop a better understanding of your limitations or your weaknesses. Although we often do not like to admit them or look at them, we all have limitations. The key is to understand what these are, recognize them and integrate them so that they no longer wittingly or unwittingly affect you. It is important that you be brutally honest with yourself in this workshop. 

Activity

In your journal, write out the answers to the following questions:

What are you not good at? Where do you fall short? Where are you not seeing the risks in your life, in general? Where are you blind to these risks and limitations?

Just as you did in the last workshop, ask three people (they can be the same people as the last workshop) that you are close with to share with you what they consider to be your main limitations, your setbacks, or your weaknesses. Compare these lists with the list that you have compiled through the meditation. However, it is important to be very clear with your confidents that this exercise is a one-time activity. This is the only time that they are invited to comment on your limitations. It would be inappropriate for any of your confidents to use this opportunity against you at some point in the future. They are doing this to help you with your inner growth not to potentially use it in a harmful way later. 

At the completion of this workshop, you will have a better understanding of your main skills and limitations.

It is important to mention that just because you have limitations it does not mean that you cannot focus your attention on improving them. The intention of this workshop is so that you can become better aware of any limitations that you may have so that they can be addressed accordingly.

name: Blockages
text:
Blockages can come in many forms that can be hindering you. These may include feeling unworthy or not good enough. They can stem from childhood and trauma. These blockages may manifest in ways where you experience guilt and shame by becoming successful, for example. In other words, you may have experienced, in your youth through your interactions with caregivers, educators, or the media, someone being shamed for their success. 

Blockages can be at the conscious level whereby you are aware of them – or they could be functioning at a subconscious level whereby you are unaware of them – they are solely impacting you at a sublevel of awareness. By accessing the subconscious through meditation, you can access vital information that you might not be aware of at the conscious level. This information can help you to better understand your underlying desires, motivations, and preconceptions.

In this workshop, we will take you through a meditation that will allow your subconscious to bring any potential blockages forward. With these blockages understood, you can delve deeper into them to understand them and to subsequently rewire them through neuroplasticity. 

Activity

In your journal, write out the answers to the following questions:

Where in your life are you experiencing blockages? List all the blocks that came up for you in this workshop.

name: Rewiring each blockage
text:
By accessing the subconscious through meditation, you can see and understand the blockage, trauma, and wounds. Once you understand where your blockages are you can rewire them through neuroplasticity. Neuroplasticity simply involves changing the brain through the creation of new neurons, which leads to new circuits that can shift you out of your default mode of operation. This means that you override the previous memory by visualizing an alternative outcome, a more optimal outcome than what really happened. For example, if you were bullied as a child, you might have developed lower self-confidence by not standing up for yourself. You can override this memory by creating an alternative outcome whereby you stand up for yourself against the bully by taking your power back. When you hear the prompt "Rewire this memory now to achieve the most optimal outcome" this is what you do. By doing this, you are not eliminating a memory, but rather changing its effect on your subconscious – you are effectively telling your subconscious what you want it to believe. 

Activity

It is recommended that all the blockages that were uncovered in the previous workshop be run through this workshop individually. To fully rewire those blockages, it is recommended to revisit this workshop, regularly. 

For the block that you discovered in the previous workshop, answer the following questions in your journal: 

When were other times that you experienced this block? When was the first time that you experienced this block? What is at the root of that block?

name: Vision
text:
In the following modules, you start by first getting a firm idea of your vision of your life and your values. With this knowledge, you then will get into discovering your passion. The first step in the process of finding your passion involves understanding, at a broad level, the vision that you have for your life. 

Activity

In your journal, write out the answers to the following questions: 

What do you want to achieve in this life? How do you want to live? What is important to you?

name: Values
text:
The second step to finding your passion is to understand your values. Values are fundamental beliefs that individuals find important. Values are vital as they act as guiding principles to how you wish to live your life. If anything that you encounter be that professionally or personally that contradicts your values or does not resonate with your values, should be rejected. Many issues that arise in an organization or relationship can be tied to a misalignment of values. It is important that job seekers and, also human resources managers, ensure that there is value alignment when employment is being offered or accepted. 

In this workshop, we will take you through a meditation and ask your subconscious to bring forward your most important values. 

Activity

In your journal, write out the answers to the following questions: 

What do you believe is important in life? What do you believe is an absolute must that you need in your: employment, primary relationship, family, and friendship? List all your personal and professional values.

name: Finding your passion
text:
Now that you know what your vision is and what your values are, we can now discover your passion. In this workshop, we will go through an activity and a meditation. In the first step, you will list all the things that you love to do, which should be aligned with your vision and values. In the second step, you will go through a meditation and allow your subconscious to bring forward anything that you might have consciously overlooked. 

Activity

In the first step, create a list of all the things that you love to do in your journal. There should not be more than 15 items on the list. Next, narrow the list down by asking yourself what is more passionate (or important) to you the first or the second item. Now, with your choice set between the first two, take the winner down to the third item and so on. If you get stuck, try to envision your life without one of the two options. Whatever you simply cannot live without is the winner. Once you have gone through your entire list and you have only one item remaining, we will next go through the meditation.

In the meditation, we will ask your subconscious to bring forward the item that your soul is most passionate about. It is important to compare this with your written responses. If there is inconsistency between your conscious list or your meditation, that is OK, it just means that you need to spend more time on it. It is perfectly normal to go through this activity a few times before you get settled on your passion. Depending on how this process develops, you may also need to revisit your vision.

name: Passion integration
text:
Now that you have a good idea of what your passion is, in this workshop, we will reflect back on your skills and limitations within the context of your passion through an activity and meditation. In a perfect world, our skills and limitations would align seamlessly with our passion, but this is not always the case. The objective of this workshop is to align your passion with your skills. If there is a skill gap, take a look at what you need to upskill to help you to get one step closer to your passion. 

Activity

For this activity take out the list of skills and limitations that you compiled earlier. Reflect back on your skills and limitations within the context of your passion and in your journal, write out the answers to the following questions: 

To reach your passion, do you live in the right location and have the right training? If your skills do not match perfectly with your passion, what do you need to do to get your there? Who can you work with (or under) to develop those skills? Who would be a perfect mentor for you or a role model? Find role models that have the traits and the skills that you need. Role models are important to our subconscious as they allow us to see those that are like us, perhaps from the same circumstances, do the things that we want to do. It shows us the possibility within ourselves.

If your skills match your passion, what steps do you need to take to get you closer to living your passion? Write out each step.

name: Empathize the pain – Part 1
text:
The first stage of design thinking involves 'empathizing the pain', which is broken up into two parts. In the first part of this process, you will keep track of various annoyances or problems that you personally encounter throughout your day. Ideally, these should be somehow tied to your passion. It is a good idea to develop a list over at least a few days to a full week. 

Activity

List all the annoyances and problems that you encountered over a few days to a week. With this list, you will then approach others, such as important stakeholders (e.g., potential customers, community members, beneficiaries, or others) and talk to them about these problems. You will empathize with them the pain that they are experiencing related to the problems that you have identified. 

With this list, we will go through a meditation to assess what are the most important problems that are emerging from your subconscious. At the completion of this meditation, you should have no more than two potential problems to investigate further. It is important that these annoyances or problems be tied to your passion. As mentioned, entrepreneurship can be a long and difficult process. If one is not passionate about their venture, it can become even more challenging to get through the long hours, the uncertainty, and the financial challenges.
explanation_video: Module 9. Empathize the pain – Part 1/Module 9. V.mp4
meditation_video: Module 9. Empathize the pain – Part 1/Module 9. M.mp4

name: Empathize the pain – Part 2
text:
Building on the list of problems that you narrowed down from the previous workshop, in the second part of this workshop, you will investigate this problem further to see if others share in the same pain that you have experienced.  

Activity

Now with your list narrowed down, you will communicate with important stakeholders to understand if they also share the same problems as you. Throughout this stage and the entire design thinking method, as a whole, entrepreneurs communicate, using empathy, with potential customers to understand the problems that they are experiencing. It is recommended that you keep good notes of the information that prospective customers provide you as you will be reflecting back on this information in future modules. 

Some schools of thought believe it is important to talk to as many people as possible. I know of some entrepreneur trainers that suggest that entrepreneurs need to talk to at least 100 people. In my view, I feel that this is excessive as you have probably reached the saturation point, which is the point where people start to tell you the same things over and over again. I have noticed that the saturation point is often at about 10 people. If you want to talk to 100 people, by all means do it, but we all have limited resources with time being one of them. 

At the conclusion of this stage, you should have a good idea if others share the problems that you identified and you will ultimately select one problem. If after this process, you find that none of your problems were considered important by prospective customers, you can 'fail' them and start the process over. It is important to mention that it is perfectly normal to restart this process many times. Design thinking is not a linear process. If you have difficulty selecting one problem to pursue, that is perfectly normal. Just spend some time reflecting deeply on it. Run it through a meditation to see what your subconscious wants you to do.

Remember, you are not to be thinking about solutions to the problems that you have identified. You are only focusing on the problems at this stage. The solutions come much later in the process.
explanation_video: Module 10. Empathize the pain – Part 2/Module 10. V.mov

name: Define the problem - Part 1
text:
The define the problem workshop in the design thinking process is divided into two parts. 

Activity

In the first part, with the one problem that you selected at the conclusion of the empathy stage, you will try defining the problem. When you have defined the problem, you will continue to communicate with important stakeholders, to see if you have defined the problem adequately. It may take you a few times before you get the definition right. Remember to take good notes from your interactions with stakeholders.
explanation_video: Module 11. Define the problem - Part 1/Module 11. V.mov

name: Define the problem – Part 2
text:
Once the problem has been defined properly, in the second part of the 'define the problem' workshop, you will speak with prospective customers to assess whether their problem is currently being solved. If the problem is not being solved, check to see if they are using a 'work around' or a 'hack' solution that alleviates the problem. If after the 'work around' or 'hack' solution their problem remains unsolved, there might be an untapped market for you to investigate further.

Activity

List all the 'work around' and 'hack' solutions that prospective customers have told you about. Keep good notes as you will be reflecting back on this information in future workshops. 

What does your subconscious want you to know about this problem?
explanation_video: Module 12. Define the problem – Part 2/Module 11. V.mp4
meditation_video: Module 12. Define the problem – Part 2/Module 12. M.mp4

name: Solution matches – Part 1
text:
Now that your problem is defined and that solving it appears to be an untapped market, you can start ideating potential solutions. In this workshop, which is divided into two parts, you will go through an activity and a meditation to allow your subconscious to bring forward potential solutions to the problem that you might not have considered. 

As mentioned, this is the first stage where you should be developing solutions. Design thinking is not a framework where you take an existing solution and run it through the process. Design thinking is all about taking a fresh start, using a blank slate. However, in many business contexts, entrepreneurs have been overly-focused on attempting to develop solutions, in the first instance, and matching these to problems that potentially do not exist after. Using the design thinking methodology, this potentially wasteful approach is circumvented by focusing on understanding the problem, first, and subsequently developing a solution after.
 
Activity

List all the potential solutions to the problem that you have identified. Compare this list with the list of 'work around' and 'hack' solutions that prospective customers have told you in the previous workshop. Keep this list for the second part of this workshop.

name: Solution matches – Part 2
text:
With the list of potential solutions that you have identified from the previous workshop, in the second half of this workshop, go back out and talk to potential customers to assess their feedback on these solutions. 

If after this process, you find that none of your solutions were considered important by prospective customers, you can 'fail' those solutions and start the ideate process over. It is perfectly normal to restart this process many times. Design thinking is a non-linear process.

If your potential customers liked one of your solutions, you have enough information to take this forward into the next stage where you will develop the solution in the form of a product or service.

name: Prototype and Test – Part 1
text:
If your problem/solution match is developed, which should have been validated by talking to many potential customers, it is time to enter the rapid prototype stage, which is divided into two parts.

Activity

The first step and goal in this stage is to develop a working prototype of your product or service in the form of a minimum viable product. A minimum viable product or a prototype are working (or beta) versions of a product or service that have just enough of the essential features to satisfy early adopting customers. Minimum viable products are a good source for feedback for future developmental work.

In this stage, by constantly communicated with potential consumers, you attempt to fail product and service features quickly to ultimately get closer to a minimum viable product that would be attractive to prospective customers. This activity, and the first part of this workshop, ends when your minimum viable product has been developed and accepted, satisfactorily by customers. This is often identified through preorders or early sales.
explanation_video: Module 15. Prototype and Test – Part 1/Module 15. V.mov

name: Prototype and Test - Part 2
text:
Activity

With your minimum viable product developed, in the second half of this workshop, we need to identify any potential barriers to the successful implementation of this minimum viable product. In your journal, explore the following questions:

What is the biggest barrier to the successful implementation of this minimum viable product (inside of you and outside)? List all the internal barriers (inside you) and external barriers (outside of you). 

Depending on what is uncovered in this workshop around potential internal barriers, it is important that you run them 'rewiring blockages' module several times to ensure that you integrate any potential blockages as these can impede your process.
